content.paragraph: In this section we start with the basic functions we discussed in Section 1.2 and obtain new functions by shifting, stretching, and reflecting their graphs. We also show how to combine pairs of functions by the standard arithmetic operations and by composition.

subsection.title: Transformations of Functions
subsection.paragraph: By applying certain transformations to the graph of a given function we can obtain the graphs of related functions. This will give us the ability to sketch the graphs of many functions quickly by hand. It will also enable us to write equations for given graphs.

Let’s first consider translations of graphs. If $$c$$ is a positive number, then the graph of $$y = f(x) + c$$ is just the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ shifted upward a distance of $$c$$ units (because each $$y$$-coordinate is increased by the same number $$c$$ ). Likewise, if $$g(x) = f(x - c)$$ , where $$c > 0$$ , then the value of $$g$$ at $$x$$ is the same as the value of $$f$$ at $$x - c$$ ($$c$$ units to the left of $$x$$ ). Therefore the graph of $$y = f(x - c)$$ is just the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ shifted $$c$$ units to the right (see Figure 1).

subsection.paragraph: Now let’s consider the stretching and reflecting transformations. If $$c > 1$$ , then the graph of $$y = cf(x)$$ is the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ stretched by a factor of $$c$$ in the vertical direction (because each $$y$$-coordinate is multiplied by the same number $$c$$ ). The graph of $$y = - f(x)$$ is the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ reflected about the $$x$$-axis because the point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is replaced by the point $$\left( {x, - y} \right)$$ . (See Figure 2 and the following chart, where the results of other stretching, shrinking, and reflecting transformations are also given.)

figure.caption: Stretching and reflecting the graph of f
figure.alt_text: Four different transformations of a curve are displayed on the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes are unmarked. The curve labeled y = f(x) begins above the positive x axis in the first quadrant, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches a high point, then goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches a low point, and again goes up and to the right. This curve y = f(x) is reflected about the x axis and the new curve thus formed in the fourth quadrant is labeled y = negative f(x). The curves y = f(x) and y = negative f(x) are equidistant from the x axis such that the low point of y = negative f(x) is located directly below the high point of y = f(x), and the high point of y = negative f(x) is located directly below the low point of y = f(x). The curve y = f(x) is reflected about the y axis and the new curve thus formed in the second quadrant is labeled y = f(negative x). The curves y = f(x) and y = f(negative x) are equidistant from the y axis such that the high point of y = f(negative x) is located directly to the left of the high point of y = f(x), and the low point of y = f(negative x) is located directly to the left of the low point of y = f(x). A curve, which has the same shape as the curve y = f(x), is drawn above it but is taller and a little narrower than f(x). This curve is labeled y = c f(x) where c > 1. Another curve, which has the same shape as the curve y = f(x), is drawn below it, but is shorter and a little wider than y = f(x), and is labeled y = (1/c) f(x). The high points of y = f(x), y = c f(x), and y = (1/c) f(x) lie on the same vertical line. Similarly, the low points of y = f(x), y = c f(x), and y = (1/c) f(x) lie on the same vertical line.

subsection.paragraph: Figure 3 illustrates these stretching transformations when applied to the cosine function with $$c = 2$$ . For instance, in order to get the graph of $$y = 2\cos x$$ we multiply the $$y$$-coordinate of each point on the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ by $$2$$ . This means that the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ gets stretched vertically by a factor of $$2$$ .

problem.paragraph: Solution Notice that each curve resembles a shifted and stretched sine function. By looking at the blue curve we see that, at the latitude of Philadelphia, daylight lasts about $$14.8$$ hours on June 21 and $$9.2$$ hours on December 21, so the amplitude of the curve (the factor by which we have to stretch the sine curve vertically) is $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {14.8 - 9.2} \right) = 2.8$$ .

By what factor do we need to stretch the sine curve horizontally if we measure the time $$t$$ in days? Because there are about $$365$$ days in a year, the period of our model should be $$365$$ . But the period of $$y = \sin t$$ is $$2\pi$$ , so the horizontal stretching factor is $$2\pi \slash 365$$ .

We also notice that the curve begins its cycle on March 21, the $$80$$th day of the year, so we have to shift the curve $$80$$ units to the right. In addition, we shift it $$12$$ units upward. Therefore we model the length of daylight in Philadelphia on the $$t$$ th day of the year by the function

subsection.paragraph: Another transformation of some interest is taking the absolute value of a function. If $$\left. y = \middle| f(x) \right|$$ , then according to the definition of absolute value, $$y = f(x)$$ when $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ and $$y = - f(x)$$ when $$f(x) < 0$$ . This tells us how to get the graph of $$\left. y = \middle| f(x) \right|$$ from the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ : the part of the graph that lies above the $$x$$-axis remains the same, and the part that lies below the $$x$$-axis is reflected about the $$x$$-axis.

problem.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the function $$y = \left| {x^{2} - 1} \right|$$ .

Solution We first graph the parabola $$y = x^{2} - 1$$ in Figure 10(a) by shifting the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ downward $$1$$ unit. We see that the graph lies below the $$x$$-axis when $$- 1 < x < 1$$ , so we reflect that part of the graph about the $$x$$-axis to obtain the graph of $$y = \left| {x^{2} - 1} \right|$$ in Figure 10(b).

subsection.paragraph: Two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ can be combined to form new functions $$f + g$$ , $$f - g$$ , $$fg$$ , and $$f \slash g$$ in a manner similar to the way we add, subtract, multiply, and divide real numbers.

subsection.paragraph: If the domain of $$f$$ is $$A$$ and the domain of $$g$$ is $$B$$ , then the domain of $$f + g$$ (and the domain of $$f - g$$ ) is the intersection $$A \cap B$$ because both $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ have to be defined. For example, the domain of $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ is $$A = \lbrack 0,\infty)$$ and the domain of $$g(x) = \sqrt{2 - x}$$ is $$B = ( - \infty,2\rbrack$$ , so the domain of $$(f + g)(x) = \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{2 - x}$$ is $$A \cap B = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ .

The domain of $$fg$$ is also $$A \cap B$$ . Because we can’t divide by $$0$$ , the domain of $$f \slash g$$ is $$\left\{ x \in A \cap B \middle| g(x) \neq 0 \right\}$$ . For instance, if $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$g(x) = x - 1$$ , then the domain of the rational function $$\left( {f \slash g} \right)(x) = x^{2} \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 1 \right\}$$ , or $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right) \cup \left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ .

There is another way of combining two functions to obtain a new function. For example, suppose that $$y = f(u) = \sqrt{u}$$ and $$u = g(x) = x^{2} + 1$$ . Since $$y$$ is a function of $$u$$ and $$u$$ is, in turn, a function of $$x$$ , it follows that $$y$$ is ultimately a function of $$x$$ . We compute this by substitution:
The procedure is called composition because the new function is composed of the two given functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ .

In general, given any two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ , we start with a number $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ and calculate $$g(x)$$ . If this number $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ , then we can calculate the value of $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ . Notice that the output of one function is used as the input to the next function. The result is a new function $$h(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ obtained by substituting $$g$$ into $$f$$ . It is called the composition (or composite) of $$f$$ and $$g$$ and is denoted by $$f \circ g$$ (“$$f$$ circle $$g$$ ”).

subsection.paragraph: The domain of $$f \circ g$$ is the set of all $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ such that $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ . In other words, $$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)$$ is defined whenever both $$g(x)$$ and $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ are defined. Figure 11 shows how to picture $$f \circ g$$ in terms of machines.

The reserve and residue volumes of air that remain in the lungs occupy about $$2000$$ mL and a single respiratory cycle for an average human takes about $$4$$ seconds. Find a model for the total volume of air $$V(t)$$ in the lungs as a function of time.
